solution:
Let \(I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{1}{2}} \dfrac{dx}{(1 - 2x^{2})\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}\)

Put \(x = \sin\theta\). Then \(dx = \cos\theta\,d\theta\).

Limits: when \(x = 0\), \(\sin\theta = 0\), so \(\theta = 0\); when \(x = \dfrac{1}{2}\), \(\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{2}\), so \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\).

Over \(0 \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{\pi}{6}\) we have \(\cos\theta > 0\), so \(\sqrt{1 - x^{2}} = \sqrt{1 - \sin^{2}\theta} = \sqrt{\cos^{2}\theta} = \cos\theta\).

Also \(1 - 2x^{2} = 1 - 2\sin^{2}\theta = \cos 2\theta\).

\(\therefore I = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \dfrac{\cos\theta\,d\theta}{\cos 2\theta \cdot \cos\theta} = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \dfrac{d\theta}{\cos 2\theta} = \displaystyle\int_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}} \sec 2\theta\;d\theta\)

Now \(\displaystyle\int \sec u\;du = \log|\sec u + \tan u|\), since multiplying and dividing by \(\sec u + \tan u\) gives

\(\displaystyle\int \sec u\;du = \displaystyle\int \dfrac{\sec u(\sec u + \tan u)}{\sec u + \tan u}\;du = \displaystyle\int \dfrac{\sec^{2}u + \sec u\tan u}{\sec u + \tan u}\;du\),

whose numerator is the derivative of its denominator, so the value is \(\log|\sec u + \tan u|\).

With \(u = 2\theta\), \(du = 2\,d\theta\):

\(I = \left[\dfrac{1}{2}\log|\sec 2\theta + \tan 2\theta|\right]_{0}^{\frac{\pi}{6}}\)

At \(\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{6}\): \(2\theta = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\), \(\sec\dfrac{\pi}{3} = 2\) and \(\tan\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \sqrt{3}\).

At \(\theta = 0\): \(\sec 0 = 1\) and \(\tan 0 = 0\), so \(\log|1 + 0| = \log 1 = 0\).

\(\therefore I = \dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(2 + \sqrt{3}\right) - \dfrac{1}{2}\log 1 = \dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(2 + \sqrt{3}\right)\)

Numerically, \(2 + \sqrt{3} \approx 3.732\) and \(\log 3.732 \approx 1.3170\), so \(I \approx 0.658\).

Check by bounding the integrand on \(\left[0, \dfrac{1}{2}\right]\), an interval of length \(0.5\). The integrand increases on this interval: at \(x = 0\) it is \(\dfrac{1}{1 \times 1} = 1\), and at \(x = \dfrac{1}{2}\) it is \(\dfrac{1}{\left(1 - \dfrac{1}{2}\right)\sqrt{1 - \dfrac{1}{4}}} = \dfrac{1}{0.5 \times 0.866} \approx 2.31\). So the value of the integral must lie between \(0.5 \times 1 = 0.5\) and \(0.5 \times 2.31 \approx 1.15\); the value \(0.659\) lies in that range.
note: Half of log(2 + sqrt 3) is 0.65848, which rounds to 0.658, not 0.659.
